subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS
speechtext:
With the indulgence of the house I should like to make a statement concerning the dumping of footwear at the Point St. Charles dump in Montreal.
On Friday, August 9, during the discussion of the foreign exchange control board bill, the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to the dumping of footwear on the Point St. Charles dump. In particular he referred to a report contained in the Montreal Star of August 8, 1946, as having stated that the Department of National Defence knew but
WarAssets-Ar7ny Supplies

would not tell the names of its officials who were responsible for the destruction of shoes, although such information was known to the department. On his making this statement I replied that I had not yet seen the article but that the department had not refused to name any of its officials; that a thorough investigation had been made; that a complete report was available and that I would make a full statement at the appropriate time, adding that I did not consider that this was during the discussion of the foreign exchange control board bill.
On reading the article I found that the statement was to the effect that the department had refused to reveal the names of the civilian dealers responsible for the dumping of the footwear. So far as I can ascertain, the Department of National Defence has not refused to divulge these names, and my understanding was that the names were furnished to the press by my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), a week or ten days ago.
When the matter of the alleged dumping of footwear on the Point St. Charles dump in Montreal was first brought to the attention of the military authorities through an article which appeared in the Montreal Daily Star of July 10, a court of inquiry was immediately set up to look into the whole matter. The court assembled on July 12, the president being Lieutenant-Colonel H. E. Vautelet, and the members, Captain A. E. Jenner, Captain S. P. Dunham and Captain J. A. Forget. A number of witnesses were examined and an exhaustive inquiry conducted into the whole matter, as a result of which it was ascertained that the footwear dumped on the Point St. Charles dump was part of approximately twenty tons of scrap leather, mixed with canvas shoes, purchased on April 25, 1946 from War Assets Corporation scrap division, Montreal, by Gorodensky Registered of 101 Ontario street east, Montreal, for a price of some $40, being at. the rate of $2 a ton. An official of the purchasing concern testified that the material had been purchased in anticipation, of disposing of it as scrap rubber or scrap leather, that upon arrival of the material it had been examined and found that the leather and rubber were mixed together and that the purchaser was unable to sell it without separating the two. As the cost of labour would be more than that which could be recovered from the material, he decided to dispose of it by throwing it out on the Point St. Charles dump.
The court of inquiry clearly established that the military authorities had nothing to do with either the sale or dumping of the footwear in question. It was also ascertained
[Mr. Abbott.!
by the court that on a previous occasion, namely, on or about May 2 or 3, another quantity of scrap material, which included scrap leather and canvas shoes purchased by Imperial Metal and Waste Company of Montreal from the J. H. Block Equipment Corporation and by the latter corporation from War Assets, had also been thrown away on the Point St. Charles dump as having been found to be unsaleable and of no commercial value.
The proceedings and the findings of the court of inquiry to which I have referred were immediately forwarded to national defence headquarters here in Ottawa, and as a result of the information contained therein, a joint statement on behalf of the Department of Reconstruction and the Department of National Defence was made at the eveining sitting on July 19 by my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction.
Subsequently on July 27, as a result of further reports that were brought to our attention, officials of War Assets Corporation, a civilian representative on my own staff and representatives from the army and Royal Canadian Air Force visited the War Assets reclamation depot at Valleyfield, Quebec. At that time various bales, bundles and bags of footwear and other articles of clothing were opened and examined to see if any articles had been mutilated or slashed. Articles which had recently arrived at the depot and which had not yet been examined by War Assets employees were examined, as well as articles which had been examined and sorted by War Assets employees, and no articles were found which had been mutilated or dashed but which were otherwise serviceable.
The seR-ice representatives requested War Assets employees at the Valleyfield reclamation depot to segregate any articles which would indicate that they had been slashed or mutilated and to advise the service representatives so that further investigations could be made in an effort to trace down the source of such mutilation. I may say that no such articles have been reported since this request was made.
Concerning the practice of War Assets Corporation, I am not in a position to make a statement, although I have a copy of a statement made to the press on the 7th of August by Mr. J. H. Berry, president of the War Assets Corporation, in which he said in part:
I must confirm that, prior to conducting this investigation, canvas shoes, which, in the opinion of the officials of the corporation, were not usable or repairable were cut by corporation inspectors at Valleyfield. This was done in accordance with previous and long-established practice. This cutting by the corporation has always been confined to footwear which, as

War Assets-Army Supplies
stated, was considered unusable and not repairable and, if it is true, as has been stated, that there were several hundred pairs of new shoes placed on the dump in a cut condition, I can find no trace of this cutting having been done by the corporation inspectors. . . .
We have now stopped cutting all canvas shoes, even when they are categorized as unrepairable and of no value in their present form as a shoe, but exactly how we are going to merchandise them as shoes, we do not yet know as we believe there will be some difficulty in finding a market for them other than as scrap.
The point as to whether it is fair policy for the corporation to sell at scrap prices unrepairable. unusable, and non-disinfected shoes without mutilating them remains to be considered by the corporation.
In conclusion may I say we have not been able to ascertain how or by whom the footwear dumped on the Point St. Charles dump was slashed, as is alleged to be the case, nor is there any clear indication as to how many shoes were allegedly mutilated. It has not been army practice to mutilate footwear since 1941, and no evidence has been adduced to show that there has been such mutilation by military personnel.
I realize the importance of an incident such as this which might appear to indicate a wilful waste in the handling of public property. I appreciate that this is not an appropriate time to discuss this matter in detail. I shall be glad to do so, however, when my estimates are before the house, which I hope will be within the next few days.

subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply or the Minister of National Defence if they can give any reason why these supplies of shoes or shirts which were alleged to have been dumped could not have been sent to Europe for relief over there?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS
speechtext: May I explain that the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has gone to great expense for years to maintain a repair depot at Valleyfield. Any footwear or clothing coming from the army which is capable of being repaired1 is being repaired by War Assets Corporation and is being sent to Europe. The discussion in the house, which has gone to great length, has to do with material which the inspectors of War Assets Corporation report as not being capable of being repaired. This we sell for junk-and we seem to have done better than the junk dealer who bought it, because at least we made $40 from it, while the junk dealer threw it away. That is the transaction with respect to which it was suggested that a royal commission be appointed. It has nothing to do with usable material, but it has to do with material which the inspectors believe is not repairable.

subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS
speechtext: I should like to ask a question which I believe is in the minds of the Canadian people. If this stuff is not repairable or is not usable, and therefore is no good, why is it slashed?

subtopic: ARMY SUPPLIES-STATEMENT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS
speechtext:
I do not think anyone in War Assets Corporation would wish to take the responsibility for marketing shoes, or allowing
War Assets-Army Supplies

anyone else to market them, which have not been disinfected. My hon. friend must realize that shoes which have been worn do carry disease. Shoes which are regarded as marketable, and which it is intended shall be marketed either here or in Europe, are carefully disinfected. The reason that the shoes are slit is to indicate that they have not been disinfected, and in the opinion of the corporation are not suitable for marketing. That has been the practice in quartermasters' stores for centuries; particularly in respect of shoes which come in and which are not suitable for resale. This was done in the usual course by the inspectors of War Assets Corporation. We have stopped it because, while we believe it is a desirable thing to do, we are not prepared to stand the criticism. As I have said, the reason it is done is that the corporation does not wish to take the responsibility for passing on shoes which are not disinfected.

subtopic: CONTROL AND SUPERVISION-REPORT AS TO PARTICIPATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
My attention was drawn this morning to an Associated Press dispatch from Tokyo, Japan, which indicated that General MacArthur had in mind or had proposed that some of the smaller or middle powers, including Canada, would be invited to join the allied war council, which at present consists of Russia, China, Great Britain and the United States, for the supervision and control of Japan. In view of this statement I take it that some preliminary formalities have been carried on between the Canadian and United States governments, or between the Canadian government and General MacArthur, and I should be glad if the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs would make some statement to the house concerning this matter, if he is in a position to do so.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): The hon. member was kind enough to show me this dispatch, which I had not seen until a few minutes ago, and which is dated Tokyo, August 13. The first paragraph indicates that General MacArthur "to-day" which would be August 13, in Tokyo suggested the "informal and unofficial" addition of seven members, including Canada, to the allied council for Japan. No invitation has been received, and probably there would not have been time for any invitation to come in the regular way, since the alleged statement would appear to have been made in Tokyo. I see nothing in the dispatch about there having been preliminary discussions in that regard between the Canadian and United States governments, but I shall make inquiries of the permanent officers of the department as to whether there have been any such preliminary discussions, and inform the hon. gentleman thereafter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the seven items under demobilization and reconversion, which are placed under the Department of Agriculture, were discussed in a general way during the general discussion on agriculture estimates. I think we covered practically every item, but inadvertently at the end of the discussion of the general items we did not do what was done in some other departments, namely, go directly to demobilization and reconversion and pass those items. For this reason they still stand to be passed by the committee. However, probably it was just as well that that was done, because two or three other matters have come up since that time. I would call the attention of the committee

to the fact that one of those subjects-the contracts with regard to meat products, and particularly bacon-can be fully discussed under item 479, which is now before the committee. Another item which hon. members desire to discuss-or one would assume that, from questions which have arisen-is 478, which deals with the dairy products board. This will permit of discussion in connection with milk and other products. I am therefore calling item 479 at this time. It will be followed by 478. Along with those I should like to ask the privilege of calling item 375 in the Department of Trade and Commerce, with which both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I are concerned. This covers the matter of the wheat contract.
I suggest that if we open our discussion by confining ourselves first to the meat board, second to the dairy products board and third to the wheat contracts, we may be able to satisfy hon. members in connection with some questions that are now in their minds. On the other items under demobilization and reconstruction, some five in number, I should be prepared to answer any questions arising generally in connection with those matters. We would first have a general discussion on the items I have mentioned, proceeding from one to the other. We might confine our discussion to the three important matters embraced by these, and then deal with the general situation under the other items. If that is satisfactory I shall proceed on that plan.
My reason for asking . the committee to agree to this procedure is that, as Minister of Agriculture I have been asked to proceed to the food conference to be held in Copenhagen on September 2. In addition I was asked some months ago by His Worship the Mayor of Dieppe to accept membership on a committee having to do with a monument to be erected to the honour of Canadians who served at Dieppe on August 19 four years ago. Within the last two weeks I have had a special invitation from the mayor of Dieppe to be the guest of Dieppe on the occasion of the laying of the cornerstone of that monument on Monday next. Since I was going to Europe anyway to attend the food conference I have planned to leave on Friday and fly to Europe and remain there for the conference. I am suggesting this means of getting right at the items with which I think hon. members are concerned, and with which I am concerned as Minister of (Agriculture, in order that we may deal with them to-day and to-morrow morning, if it is necessary to go into to-morrow morning, in order that they may be fully covered while I am still in the house. If it meets with the approval of the committee I

Supply-Agriculture-Demobilization
shall move down with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and proceed to discuss them in that way.
As to item 479, dealing with the meat board, a question was asked in my absence the other day with regard to the contracts which have been entered into between Britain and Denmark and their relation to the contract which we have with Britain for the deliver}' of bacon to that country. I do not think it is necessary for me to go into the details of the contract which we have with Britain, other than to say that we have had contracts for the sale of bacon and ham to Great Britain ever since the fall of 1939 when the war began. Under those contracts we have delivered considerable quantities of bacon and ham to Britain.
The contracts started out with quantities much lower than have been provided in recent contracts. The highest amount we undertook to deliver under those contracts was in 1943. Since that time the amounts contained in the contracts have been reduced to 450 million pounds. The contract for the last two years has been a contract calling for the delivery of at least 450 million pounds. In one of those years we delivered1 more than that amount; in one year I think we delivered almost that amount, and this year we are not hopeful of being able to deliver that amount.
Under the contract entered into we have agreed to a reduction in the quantity that we are required to deliver to at least 350 million pounds. In 1948 we have agreed to attempt to deliver 400 million pounds. In other words we believe that we can increase deliveries in 1948 over the deliveries in 1947 and therefore we have entered into a contract under which we agree to deliver a greater quantity in 1948 than in 1947.
I think it is in order to explain the position which the government took in relation to the discussions which have taken place and the contract which resulted therefrom covering the years 1946, 1047 and 1948. The 1946 price was arranged at $22.50 per hundred pounds. One should distinguish between a hundred pounds in Canadian terms and a hundredweight in British terms, because the failure to make that distinction has resulted in wrong information being published in the press with regard to the difference between the price that is being obtained- by Denmark and the price that is obtained1 by Canada in connection with this contract. Discussions with regard to our contracts have usually been in terms of Canadian hundred pounds, but when Britain is discussing a contract of that kind it is always discussed in terms of the British
hundredweight, which is 112 pounds. That has resulted in misunderstanding in discussing the price that is being obtained.
By way of laying a background, I should like to say that we have no official information, other than what has been in the press, with regard to the actual terms of the agreement with Denmark. We have been attempting to get official returns from the British representatives here, and they have been attempting to get them in Britain, but what- I am going to give this morning is the closest possible estimate that we could arrive at from the press reports and from the information we have been able to obtain directly from the British officials here as to what is contained in the Danish contract.
Before giving these figures, I should like to point out that in relation to farm products and the prices to foe obtained for them we have laid down a definite policy which has been discussed in this house on a number' of occasions. We have had two objectives in mind. One is to maintain our marketings of farm food products in Britain at the highest possible levels made possible by the production which we have in Canada. We have attempted to avoid giving wrong information to the British as to what food would be supplied or could be supplied from year to year. Then we have written into the contracts the highest quantities that we felt sure we could deliver to the British.
Taking that into consideration we have not been prepared to agree that Canada ought to accept, even if it were suggested-and I am not saying it has been suggested-a constant reduction in the quantities contained in our contracts, beginning say with the first year after the war and continuing downward through the years following the war. We have taken the position in arranging prices, that we should not agree to ask our people to accept a gradual reduction in price for any product which we are selling to the British. I think it would give an indication to our people, to our producers particularly, if we were to agree to contracts with a gradual reduction in quantity and a gradual reduction in price, that we were being asked by the British or by other countries in which we might be marketing farm products to get back gradually to a position in which we would be marketing lesser quantities at a lower return. In all our discusisons we have attempted to maintain the position that we would have a stabilized price and a stabilized minimum quantity to be delivered into the British market over a period of time.
With these thoughts in mind I should like to make some comparison between the contract between Britain and Denmark as we
4780	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Demobilization
understand it, and the contract which we ourselves have arranged with the British people for the marketing of bacon and ham in Great Britain. The present arrangement between Great Britain and Canada provides for a price for Canadian bacon f.o.b. Canadian port of 825 per 100 pounds for 1046 and through from January to August of 1947. I use those months because as I understand it the Danish contract begins with September 1 and continues through until August 31, 1947. So taking that full year, beginning in Canada with September and continuing through to August, the Canadian price is $25 in Canada per 100 pounds. That Canadian price does not include the $1 per hundred which is paid by the federal government on A hogs by way of premium and 50 cents per 100 pounds which is paid on B hogs, nor does it include any subsidies that may also be paid by the provincial governments. The $25 per 100 pounds is the price obtained for Canadian bacon and ham at Saint John or Montreal for the product purchased by Great Britain. That price * continues down to August 31, 1947.
The Danish price for the same period for 100 pounds-not 112 pounds-f.o.b. Danish port is $26.98, which is $1.98 higher than the Canadian price for the same period. That price of $26.98 continues down to September 1, 1947. Then from September to December, 1947, while the Canadian price is a flat price of $25 right through for all of 1946 and down to August 31, 1947, the price under the Danish contract is $25.19 per one hundred pounds beginning September 1 and continuing until the end of December. In other words, it is 19 cents higher than the price which we obtain in Canada for 100 pounds.
I come now to the year 1948. Remember that in 1947 we are to deliver 350 million pounds to Great Britain at $25 per 100 pounds, and in 1948, 400 million pounds, at a price yet to be determined. We are to determine that price some months in advance of Jaunary 1, 1948. But there is a floor placed under the Canadian price. The British have agreed that we shall not be asked to accept less than we were getting at the time, the contract was changed in 1946 from $22.50 to $25. So that the floor for 1948 is $22.50, with the possibility of negotiating for a higher return for the bacon which we provide for Great Britain in 1948.
The price under the Danish contract for 1948 is $21.59 at a Danish port. That is, it is very much lower than ours.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: Is that a fixed or floor price?

That is the price they are selling at. So far as we know, and I do not want to be too definite, those are the prices which have been stated in the press and which have been agreed to by the British officials here to be the price which they think is in the contract with Denmark. That is the information upon which any news items which have been written have been based, and the information is that the Danish price for 1948 will be $21.59. In other words, the Danish price starts out at $26.98 and gradually goes down to $2199. I might point out that we in our discussions did not desire to enter into a contract which started out at a high level and went down to a lower level, particularly if we could get an average price throughout the period which would net us as much over the entire period as varying prices would have netted us, and we obtained that. The British fully understand our position, and I would judge from the figures here that they have taken into consideration the discussions they had with us when entering into a contract with Denmark, and they have not given Denmark any advantage whatsoever over us. There may be some conditions existing in Denmark which would have made it advisable and perhaps preferable for Denmark to ask for a higher price in the year immediately following the war and to be prepared to take a lower price later on.

I still take exception to what the minister said. 1 come from an area in Saskatchewan where we produce a lot of live stock. Our hog production in that area was high in the early part of the war. We paid out hundreds of thousands of dollars last year to store grain in the elevators at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Calgary and Edmonton, to prevent its being shipped out of there at all, to keep it there to feed live stock in that area; and it has all been fed. We cannot find any barley. There is a small quantity of oats that we could ship out, but we cannot find any barley or any feed wheat to ship anywhere, whether outside Canada or inside Canada. The situation is that the grain has been fed. Well, if it has been fed, I do not see how you could feed any more live stock, no matter what you did. If it is a question of thinking that we ought to have more feed grown in Canada, probably we could get more feed grown by following some practices; but again, that would not meet the wishes of a lot of people who just a few months ago were saying that we ought to be growing wheat to the exclusion of other things, in order to feed people somewhere else in the world.
I agree with hon. members who have spoken that we have to pay a little more attention to the people who live in our own country than some of us have been tending to do in the last few months. To say that we should not grow any grain in western Canada to ship to eastern Canada is, I think, going a long way. I do not think it is a bad thing for the farmers in western Canada, when we give them the extra ten or fifteen cents on their oats and) barley. Up to that time we were getting 67 per cent of our share of the income of the farmers of Canada as based on experience of 1926-29; and when we put the fifteen cents on barley and the ten cents on oats, and put up the initial price of wheat,

we got into the position that we should occupy in relation to other farmers. We are a grain producing area. Grain is the natural thing for us to produce, and we can produce it. We have to have a market for it, and the best market for our feed grains is in western Canada. At the present time the best market would be in the United States, but if the grain went to them you would not be able to feed hogs either in eastern or western Canada. Usually the best market has been in the east, and we have been promoting the shipment of our grain from west to east. As long as we keep our present controls I do not think we can market it, to the advantage of the people generally, anywhere else.
I would just like to- answer the minister for one moment, when he said that I said coarse grains had been shipped out of western Canada.. You cannot have it both ways.
There are no coarse grains shipped out of the area west of the Sault line. We absolutely corralled it there.

Three or four hon. members 'have said that their areas have been large hog producing areas. My own area is similar, but I can say that farmers in our constituency with oats in their granaries have gone completely out of hogs. If we want to have mixed farming in western Canada, if we want to have what we call a stability in agriculture, and mixed farming, to which many of these areas are adapted, if not perhaps the big grain sections, we must have a policy under which the farmer can have some trust in government policies and will know over a period of years that he is going to be able to get a fair return for the type of farming he undertakes.

I believe that the retention of the British market for bacon is very important. During the first great war we did get a fair market over there; we were shipping between 126 and 135 million pounds of bacon. We did not keep that up, and I think it is very important that, since we now have that market again, we should do everything possible to retain it.
I am not finding any fault with the suggestion which has been made by our western friends that there should be some method of equalizing the prices received for hogs by the western farmer and the eastern farmer. If that can be done, well and good. On the other hand I would not like to see the freight rates which have been paid by the government up to the present time on feed grains coming from the west cut off. We cannot afford to pay the freight rates in addition to the prices

The eastern part of my constituency will probably have another crop failure, and they will have to go out of hogs because they have not got the feed.
I believe that the best way to encourage the raising of hogs is a long term policy which will guarantee the farmers a fair price for hogs over a period of time which will enable them to adopt labour-saving methods. They have the most modern labour-saving machinery with which to grow grain, but few farmers have proper facilities for handling hogs, and therefore it means a lot of labour.

When the minister was speaking this morning he mentioned the fact that more of the cheaper grades of beef were going to Great Britain, and that they were paying lower prices accordingly. I should like to know just what is the relationship between the boards enumerated here and the wartime prices and trade board. Surely the wartime prices and trade board does not set prices on farm products of all kinds without in some way consulting with these other boards which are vitally interested. I understand that the meat board particularly has to do with export prices, but I also notice that in the order in council setting up the meat board it says they are to determine prices to be paid packers or other persons, and as well to establish differentials in prices which will be paid for different grades, selections and weights of various kinds of meats. That may be for export; perhaps that is what was intended, but it does not definitely say so. There is a real grievance at the present time on the part of the smaller slaughterers through the country, who say that because they cannot get official inspection they are not able to obtain the higher prices which are paid for the red and blue brand beef. I should like to ask the minister if this board or any of these boards have anything to do with that, or whether it is entirely a matter for the wartime prices and trade board.

Prior to 1943, I think it was, the wartime prices and trade board provided all the subsidies, that is, producer subsidies as well as consumer subsidies. In 1943 we set up the food board, which is dealt with in these estimates. Under the arrangements then made the food board provides for the subsidies to producers, what are called the producer subsidies designed to increase production, and the prices board deals with any' subsidies that are paid having to do with consumers, to keep down costs to consumers. That division was made at that time. As far as the provision of food for the Canadian people is concerned the prices board have the final authority and final responsibility. That is, they are supposed to see to it that sufficient food is left in Canada to properly feed the
Canadian people. If it is found necessary, as has been the case in connection with some products, to impose rationing, then the wartime prices and trade board looks after the rationing, and they must have the responsibility for saying whether or not sufficient food is being provided to the food distributors in Canada to make that rationing possible; and to that extent they have control. When it comes to the practical handling of it, any time we find that costs of production are not being met, or any time we feel they are not being met, the board having to do with the product in question negotiates with the prices board in order to have that situation adjusted. There are two ways in which that adjustment can be made, from our point of view. One is to give a subsidy to the producer; the other is to increase the price to the consumer so that higher returns may be obtained. Whenever it is considered necessary to get higher returns by increasing prices, that is discussed with the prices board, which makes the final order in that connection and enforces it.
That is what really happened in connection with beef. About two or three months ago there was widespread discussion as to the reasons for beef not appearing on the market. As a result of those discussions the prices board eventually raised the prices of the higher grades of beef, that is blue and red brand beef. As a result beef again began to move on to the market, in much greater quantities; and the beef has been sold practically at ceiling prices. I am informed that within the last week or two the experience has been that the Canadian people are inclined to eat beef that costs less, rather than to eat the red and blue brand beef. In other words, there is always the possibility of getting your prices so high that the consumer will say, "If I must pay that price I shall eat something else." The consumers have reached that point now, apparently, in regard to red and blue brand beef, and we are being offered beef of these higher grades to send to Britain at prices considerably below' ceiling. I just throw that out as a suggestion to those who talk nothing but price. There are limits to what you can do even in connection with price. When we start asking people to pay certain prices for commodities, they may refuse.
I was not finding any fault whatever with the price. I was trying to get some information as to the basis on which, that price is set.

Just to make that clear I would add that our boards naturally have the responsibility of seeing to it that the producer gets what is coming to him. The
