The meat board is taking these products and exporting them and 83 to 85 per cent of what they cost laid down at the point from which they are moved to Britain goes back to the farmer.
How much has the export trade been speeded up since rationing came into effect?

It would be impossible to show that there has been an increase in exports since rationing was brought in, because, as has been stated here time after time, production of hogs has been going down. The big export of meat in 1943 and 1944 was bacon. Then we switched over to a large extent from bacon to beef in 1944, and particularly in 1945. The export of beef went up considerably in the latter part of 1944 and all through 1945 and it is still quite high. The export of bacon and ham is down because production is down. The only indication one could take is that the consumption of meat in Canada is lower under rationing than it was before. We can only assume that to the extent it is lower the meat is going out of Canada because it is all being marketed.

Were the increased
exports to the United Kingdom or to the United States?
Entirely to the United Kingdom.

Coming back to the question raised by the hon. member for Battle River, can the minister make any statement as to what is being done to prevent a recurrence of what happens when farmers ship live stock to the market and find that prices fluctuate one or two cents per pound because of congestion? I know there is a floor under butcher steers and slaughter cattle, but there is no floor to the farmer. This fall there is a great likelihood that when the heavy run occurs there will be congestion at the Winnipeg market and prices will go down. As a consequence farmers one week will receive perhaps one or two cents per pound less for their cattle, which on a 1,400 pound steer may mean a loss of from $14 to $25. When farmers keep their cattle on the range or on pasture they should be guaranteed against loss when they ship better fed stock to market.

I could give figures which would indicate there is no variation in the average monthly prices through the years, but that would not answer the question the hon. member has in mind. All I can say is what I said this morning, that never at any time has the price of hogs been below what the buyers would be justified in paying for them under the floor prices that are established by these agreements. The price has always been higher than the floor under hogs. I submit that it would not be in the interests of the farmer to say that if somebody requires hogs with sufficient urgency he should not be allowed to pay a cent or two higher some weeks than someone else, and that the farmer should not be allowed to get that cent or two cents, whatever it may be. It stands to reason that if he is permitted to pay that cent or two cents for a week or two, at the end of that week or two it must come down to the average which has always been above the floor.
All we have ever sought to do is to establish a floor sufficiently high to give reasonable returns and to say that the price must not go below that floor. We have never attempted to stop them from going above. The prices board have the responsibility for seeing that the commodity as sold to the consumer is not sold above a certain price, and that usually takes care of any control that there needs to be at the top. As to whether it goes up or not, we have not attempted to

Supply-Agriculture-Demobilization____
stop that, but our regulations say that there must be a floor. We have let them do that, and of course if we do that we must let it come down again.
With regard to these fluctuations, I would say that that is more in the hands of the farmer and the gentleman who is picking up the live stock around the country. This always occurs in the latter part of September and in October because we are approaching the winter at that time. All other times it can be pretty well taken care of if the farmer is a little careful about when he ships and the buyer who is handling the stock is a little careful about when he takes it in.
I have had the same man handling my stock for the ten years I have been here and I have never found any reason to complain. He calls at my place and gets it when he thinks it ought to go out. I always take his advice because I think he knows more about it than I do. He is at the market every week or so and he knows what the market is. I have never had any complaint to make with regard to his taking the stock, and I must say that I have always been satisfied with the price when I examined the cattle, examined the hogs and examined the market. I think that is true of most of those who have been careful about the matter. I can say without fear of contradiction that there has been less variation in the price of live stock in the last five years, certainly in the last three years, than we have ever before experienced in this country.
For hew many years has there been a floor price?
We have been in this position now for two and a half years.
Is there any definite date at which it will expire?
So long as these contracts continue it will pretty well have to continue.

The minister said that from 83 to So cents of the dollar obtained for meat exported was returned to the farmer. How does he obtain those figures? Has the board examined the books of the packing houses to ascertain their costs?

On the product that I am speaking of which is exported overseas, theoretically at least, the packing house is our agent. They buy the hogs, and we know what is paid for the hogs. We know what we allow the packing plant for the bacon. We know what the costs are. We have all those figures on our own books. We know what the farmer obtains for the hogs. So that there is no danger of our just taking
figures that have been prepared by the packing houses, although I may say that jus* this week figures were given to me voluntarily by one packing house which were almost exactly the same as our own figures.
The meat board does not put auditors into the packing plants to ascertain the cost of processing?

They do not put an auditor in, but they get all these costs daily when they are buying, just as any business man would. I follow the markets all the time myself. They are on my desk every morning. When I have noticed variations between Calgary, Winnipeg and Toronto I have had Mr. Pearsall in and asked him, "Why is that?" I have said, "I want to know why it is before I will accept that position." We do that all the time in the department. Not only do I do it, but the deputy minister does it, and the director of marketing; everyone associated with it checks these things every day. It is on that check that I base my statement that hogs have not been below the floor.
I think we are getting away from the question. How does the minister arrive at the figures of the percentage that goes to the farmer and the packer?

Let me put it simply. A hog is bought in Winnipeg. We know what was paid for it on a certain day. That hog goes to the packing plant and is processed. We know what the product is that comes out as a result, because we take it, and we know what we allow for it. It is moved down to the port because delivery is taken at the port. We know the cost of moving it there. We know all these costs; we do not have to go to anybody for them, because we have them.
The figures we have been given so far refer to the product which is exported. Can the minister give us comparable figures for the product that is put on the domestic market?

Whether it goes overseas or is consumed in Canada the same price is paid to the farmer for a similar grade. He gets his percentage of that particular output. There may be times when for a short period a packing plant may pay one cent or two cents a pound more than the market permits, but I do not know where they would get any extra return by doing that because there is a ceiling price at which they have to sell, and so any extra price they pay comes off any return which they get. ft does not come off the farmer.

Supply-Agriculture-Demobilization
Is the ceiling the same for the domestic market as for the export market?
There is no ceiling on the export product. It is the floor price that is on the export product.
How does the domestic ceiling compare with that?

There is a margin
allowed. On blue beef, for example, the margin is one-quarter of one cent. The floor is just one-quarter of one cent below the ceiling, and we undertake to buy all the beef on the market at one-quarter of a cent under the ceiling. Most of the time recently we have not been able to get it. It is selling so close to the ceiling that we cannot buy it at one-quarter of one cent under the ceiling.

Friends of mine coming back from a motor trip in the United States say they were able to buy Canadian bacon over there. If that is so, would the price be higher? Would the farmer receive more for bacon sold here than for bacon going say to the United States?

There is no bacon exported legally from Canada to the United States. Some bacon may find its way over there through irregular channels. On menus in the United States there sometimes appears what is called Canadian-style bacon. It is produced from hogs similar to the hogs in Canada and cured in a similar way, but it is not Canadian bacon produced in Canada.

Item agreed to.
478. Dairy products board, $2,029,102.

I would like the minister to make a statement on the milk situation. He announced in the spring that the winter subsidy would be added to the summer price. The consumer has lost the two cents subsidy. I do not know whether the minister's department has anything to do with that or whether it comes under some other department. The milk situation all over the Dominion of Canada to-day has to be straightened out or we are not going to have sufficient milk for our people. The two cents subsidy on milk was one of the finest investments that any government ever made in the health of this nation, because milk is not only a drink but a food, containing about 800 calories per quart. The milk industry must be protected, because it would be disastrous if the dairymen began to sell off their herds which mean so much to the whole country. I would like the minister to make a statement and tell us what he intends to do with the dairy farmer this winter as far as price is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, last
spring the announcement was made that the two cent consumer subsidy was to be taken off milk. It was a decision reached after discussions which took place between the dairy board, the Department of Agriculture and the prices board, and I believe discussions took place between the prices board and the provincial milk boards who had the authority to adjust prices before the war started, and still have the legal authority under the constitution as soon as our special war regulations are taken off. There had been considerable discussion for, I would say, eighteen months before that, during most of which time the producer organizations were most anxious that the amount they were to obtain for their product should be established in the form of a price rather than that an amount of say ten cents at a certain point should be maintained as the proper price for milk and then a subsidy of two cents paid on top of that to make it possible for them to consume it. It was thought that the increase in earnings had been sufficient to warrant the two cents being taken into the price, and that was done.
In, spite of the fact that the total milk production this year i3 down two or three per cent, total sales of whole milk are up from seven to eight per cent, so that the putting of the consumer subsidy into the price has not resulted in a smaller consumption of milk; milk is being consumed in greater quantities notwithstanding that price increase. The other part of the picture is this, that we are also paying producer subsidies, and as will be remembered, we were paying thirty-five cents per hundred during the summer months and fifty-five cents during the winter months. This spring it was suggested that we should put the summer subsidy up to the same level as the winter subsidy and make it fifty-five cents, with the idea that when we came into the winter again there would be a higher return required. That was examined into very carefully and discussed very fully with producer organizations and others, and eventually we suggested that we were prepared to do a certain thing: we were not prepared to go to fifty-five cents for the summer months but we were willing to make some increase. That was not acceptable, and it was finally said'-and I do not think there was much disagreement about it-that at some time these [DOT] subsidies would have to be taken off and the control would have to go back to the provincial boards. After the discussions had taken place it was finally determined as a matter of government policy that the date at which it

Supply-Agriculture-Demobilization
should go back to the control of the provincial boards was the first of October, 1946; and so we said that for the five months we would pay fifty-five cents, in the summer months, in order to give those who were interested an opportunity of adjusting the position as between the producer and the consumer. My understanding of what was said in the house and wdiat was said in the discussions was that there was not going to be any great difficulty about taking care of the consumer subsidy plus a sufficient proportion of the producer subsidy to keep the cost to the consumer still within the range of what was thought by the prices board at that time to be a reasonable increase in the cost of living as compared with increases which were being given in earnings; and so it was thought that the matter could be properly turned over to the milk boards as of the 1st of October and that in the meantime they should work out their plans. The provincial boards are meeting in Ottawa this week-as a matter of fact they met me two days ago- and they are discussing that question. 1 do not know what decision will be reached. Yesterday morning or the day before I spent three-quarters of an hour with them before coming to the house, and I think they went from me to see the prices board people to discuss the whole position, to find out just where we were at the moment, and what effect anything they might do would have upon the general position. All I can say is that the question is being fully considered and discussed between the two authorities which have something to do with the establishing of returns. I have been in negotiation this week; final decisions have not been reached as to what is to be done. Some have suggested that a longer time should be given, and that in order to make that longer time possible some producer subsidy should still be paid- not as much as we were paying before, but that something should be paid-and that some of the extra cost should be taken over by the consumer. These questions are being discussed this week and will be determined, I assume, in sufficient time to make the announcement long enough before the first of October to acquaint people with what the situation is.

Well, that is the question which is under consideration. The agricultural prices control board which we set up two sessions ago is also working on these statistics with regard to the whole problem; and the dairy association-I think that that is the proper term to apply to it-the organization of producers, have put a man to work on it and have already presented to us their idea of what the increased costs are and of what they require in order to produce milk. All these submissions are being considered now by the proper boards; a conclusion will be finally reached and announced, and I hope it will be satisfactory when it is made.

I hope that the government the minister represents will take into consideration what milk means to this nation. When we examined the boys for this last war, many of them were found wanting, and our medical authorities tell us that had they been able to drink an abundance of milk, or even milk in regular quantities, they would have been better prepared to pass the tests. The subsidy of $20 million which we paid to enable people to buy milk is the finest investment in health this country ever made.

Up to the present time this discussion has been largely on fluid milk, its production and consumption. But usually in past years we have had a surplus of milk on our hands, and the one way, usually, in which that milk can be disposed of was in the form of cheese. As with bacon, we have built up a good market for cheese in Great Britain. I hope that we shall be able to maintain as much of that market as possible. Owing to the higher cost of production in the cheese and concentrated milk industry-and there is some of that going to Britain as well-they seem to think they are not making ends meet. In fact I understand that the production of concentrated milk has gone down some eighteen per cent. The production of cheese has also gone down considerably during the past few months.
I understand that a short time ago the concentrated milk producers' association and the Ontario cheese producers' association presented a brief to the minister showing the increased cost of production of milk and the falling off in the production of these two particular commodities, and asking for some relief. Has anything been done, or is it considered that anything will be done to

Supply-Trade and Commerce
assist these two important branches of the dairy industry, because as far as possible we must keep up our production of cheese which goes to Great Britain. Continuity of supply is one of the important factors in maintaining that market. We have the quality in the cheese and something should be done to protect that market.

With regard to the
figures used, I would call the attention of the hon. member for Haldimand to the fact that from the records the total production of condensed, evaporated and whole milk- powder is down 1-8 per cent, not 18 per cent, but cheese is down 21-1 per cent. It is a little early in the season to be too sure about the cheese position. The grass was poor in the early part of the season. It has become better recently and there may be some pick-up, but it will not pick up that much. There will be some decrease in the production of cheese.
However, I wish to say that the delegation which brought figures with regard to whole milk also brought figures with regard to cheese, canned milk and butter. We had a full discussion with regard to the matter, and the figures which were brought have been submitted to the agricultural prices control board. They are working on them at the present time. Again it is a question of a decision being reached on this matter by October 1. What the position ought to be at the moment I cannot go any farther than to say that the whole matter is under consideration. We are just as anxious as any hon. member to keep this production just as high as we can get it.
Item agreed to.

Foreign trade services-
375. Wheat and grain division, $28,532.

Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Agriculture anything further to tell the committee about the wheat agreement which was made and announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on July 25, and also in connection with the determining of the policy with regard to the prices that are to be paid to farmers on the four years' crops commencing now? What further information has the minister to give along these lines?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Some weeks ago I, in behalf of the government, made a statement in connection with the United1 Kingdom wheat agreement and also in connection with the domestic wheat policy of the government.

At that time I promised that there would be an opportunity to discuss these matters when the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce were being considered. Heretofore in our estimates we have never had any specific item under w'hich matters relating to wheat contracts or to the wheat board could be discussed, but because of the establishment of a grain division within the department during the past year we are able, on this item, to discuss matters in connection with wheat.
In answer to the question just asked by the hon. member for Battle River, I may say that I do not think I have anything to add to the- statement I have already made regarding the British contract and very little to add to the statement regarding the domestic wheat policy. There is one matter in connection with which there has been a certain amount of criticism throughout the country, namely, the domestic policy in relation to participation payments on the 1945 crop. In my statement I said that there would be upwards of sixteen cents a bushel paid in participation certificates on the 1944 wheat crop. Further consideration of the matter leads me to believe that that estimate was based on a wrong premise and that the payment on the 1944 crop will be considerably higher than the amount I suggested, namely sixteen cents a bushel, and the payment on the 1945 crop correspondingly lower.

Is that still being carried forward to 1950? The statement made by the minister was that the price would be $1.35 and an additional ten cents to apply to the 1945 crop. I am asking if that is still the intention of the government. The criticism is that the government has what amounts to a contract with the farmers of the country to pay a participation certificate on the basis of the proceeds of the crop when the crop was sold, and that this is in effect a breach of the contract. That is the criticism I have heard.

Yes. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, will deal more extensively with that point. There is no change in policy to suggest here so far as that is concerned. The initial payment will be . made to the wheat producer of $1.35 a bushel f.o.b. Fort William and the other places for the five 3'ears, the past year and the next four years. [DOT]

On behalf of this group I wish to say that we are glad to know that we are to have stabilized prices for the next four crop years and also that an agreement has been made with Britain. I am not going to say

Supply-Trade and Commerce
whether we are well satisfied with the prices received. We feel that the British government are satisfied that they got a very good deal at the expense of Canada. One of my reasons for saying that is contained in a Canadian press dispatch of July 26, which states:
The Neics-Chronicle's streamer headline said: "Strachey explains wheat deal and 11.P.'s cheer Canada."
In my opinion they had every right to cheer Canada. The dispatch goes on to say:
The Mirror headlined the story: "Pact Makes Britain's loaf safe for four years."
The Daily Graphic said editorially:	"Our
debt to the empire increases every day . . . thanks, Canada, and thanks again!"
I am glad the people of Britain appreciate that they are getting a good deal from Canada.
I might say we have no objection whatever to Canada's supplying the best food in the world to Britain and to other countries, but we object to the farmers bearing the brunt of the fexpense. On many occasions we have made it 1 clear that the farmers of Canada have not 1 received the price for their products to which they are justly entitled, I still estimate that Wthe same condition continues under the present agreement. Of course we are very well satisfied to have a stabilized price for some time to come, because we all remember what happened after the first great war and we do not want conditions of that kind to arise again; but in view of the losses the farmers accepted from 1930 up to 1942, I feel we are entitled to a much better deal as far as our wheat is concerned. I am not going to deal in particular with the sale to the British government. The cost of that will, of course, be taken care of by the government here, and we in turn will have to bear our share of the loss through taxation.
In connection with our domestic policy, in the first place I do not feel that the initial price is high enough. It is true that the initial price of SI .35 is to last for five years. We appreciate that, particularly in regard to the later years; but because between 1930 and 1942 the farmers of this country received only 16-6 per cent of the national income while comprising 33 per cent of the population, we feel that on our wheat sales alone we have lost no less than 82,200,000,000, and if that amount had been distributed among the wheat growers of Canada it would have made quite a difference in their financial standing. Again we must remember that up to August 1, 1942, we were getting a price of only seventy cents a bushel for our wheat, basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. We felt that in accepting such a price we would be recompensed when the war was over. In the price
(hat has been announced, however, we do not feel that this compensation is forthcoming. During the 1945 and 1946 crop years we are permitted unlimited deliveries, but in the three years following, if conditions warrant it, we may be cut down to fourteen bushels per authorized acre, which would mean that man}' farmers could grow much more wheat than they could deliver. I hope there will be no market restrictions to prevent the government from taking all the wheat Canadians can grow during this period.
Again, we are to have a ten cent additional payment on our 1945 crop deliveries, that is, on the wheat delivered from August 1, 1945, to July 1, 1946. That would bring us up to an initial payment of 81.35 for the year just ended, and we are to have no payment on participation certificates issued on our crops delivered between August 1, 1945, and July 31, 1950, until late in 1950. This means that the government will borrow the money of the farmers free of interest during all that time. By the time we pay our income tax, which will amount to perhaps thirty cents a bushel on amounts over and above our exemptions, that is going to cut our wheat price down pretty far. I believe that our initial _ price should be not less than $1.55 a bushel for the entire five-year period, and that participation certificates should be figured and j paid each year. Under the method the government is adopting it is possible that during the later years, if the price of our wheat goes down to SI a bushel for the last year, our initial payment of $1.35 may be our final payment; because, as has already been pointed out, on many occasions we find that the floor price is the price we receive. So that in my opinion S1.55 should be the initial price rather than SI.35; and by having participation certificates paid each year the farmer would get the benefit of any additional gains made, particularly in the early years of the contract. Otherwise the high price we may get-and I repeat "may"-in the early years may be eaten up by low prices in the later years of the contract.
This policy is being announced in face of the fact that the prices of everything we have to buy are climbing daily. From time to time we receive letters stating that prices of things in the stores are going up, and we see that a number of labour organizations are on strike to-day asking for an increase of approximately fifteen cents an hour. Similar increases have been granted in the past; and we know that the consumer class, which takes in the farmers, will have to bear the brunt of these additional wages for labour which are included in prices. I am not saying labour is not

Supply-Trade and Commerce
entitled to its due, but since the benefits to labour are being increased there is no reason in the world why the farmer should not also have his prices increased. A little later on we may be told, as we were told a couple of months ago by the Minister of Finance, that prices of farm products have increased by a very large percentage since the beginning of the war. This does not mean, however, that the financial position of the farmer has been improved very much, because at the beginning of the war we were accepting depression prices for our products; and even when you add the percentages that have been announced by the minister to prices which were far below the cost of production it does not place the farmer in an enviable position.
! With reference to the programme of supply-j ing wheat to the millers at 77$ cents a bushel, of course that is subsidized by the government to the extent of the difference between that price and the domestic price of $1.25. But again, I cannot understand why our domestic price should be $1.25. The farmers should not have to bear this burden. The domestic price should be up to at least $1.55, if not to the average selling price for each year's crop. There is no reason why the farmers should continue to subsidize the consumers of this '[DOT]country.
We are glad to see that the wheat board is to continue in operation. It has given satisfaction to all. Many of us were very glad to see that the services of the grain exchange are not being made use of. On another occasion I asked the minister whether the wheat board is continuing to pay a commission on sales of wheat to the commission merchants and brokers on the exchange, and I hope that to-day the minister will tell us that policy has been discontinued. There is no reason why it should be carried on, and it should have been stopped many months ago.
I do not think I should say very much more, though we may have further comments to make a little later on. The policy of the social crediters and our supporters is that the initial price should be $1.55 a bushel with participation certificates computed and paid annually, and we shall have more to say as the discussion goes on.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated a few minutes ago that I would have something to say with regard to this matter, and perhaps I should make that statement at this stage. My reason for saying anything at all at the moment is largely the fact that last January, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I were in Britain, we opened discussions with the British govern-

ment looking to the negotiation and signing of a contract on wheat covering a period of time. Later on in the season it became necessary to continue those discussions while the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Central America, and I represented the government in carrying on those discussions. Therefore I am familiar with some of the discussions which took place during the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce was absent.
He has suggested to me that I might give the committee the benefit of some of the conclusions reached, and the reasons for arriving at them. It will be recalled that on September 19, 1945, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a statement to the house with regard to future policy in connection with wheat. I think I should place on record at this time three paragraphs from that statement which bear upon some of the questions now being discussed, and which have been referred to by the hon. member for Battle River. In -the portion I wish to quote the following is stated:
In asking Canadian producers to forgo such benefits as might be realized in the short run through higher export prices, the government recognizes the paramount need for relative stability of income to wheat producers. Toward this end, the government undertakes that in the five-year period-
And I wish to emphasize that right in the first announcement what was spoken of was a five-year period.
ending July 31, 1950, producers will receive not less than $1 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern. in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver on the authorized deliveries for each crop year. For the balance of the 1945-16 crop year, at least, the Canadian wheat board initial advance will continue at $1.25, where it was set two years ago. By providing a long-term floor price of not less than $1 the government will protect producers against the consequences of any sharp reversal in the world wheat position during the next five-year period.
The government, in adopting this policy of a maximum price for overseas shipments for the present and a floor price for five years, is asking the producers, in their own interests, to forgo exceptional short-run advantages in favour of a long-run stability of income. In arriving at its decision on this policy, the government had the following fundamental considerations in mind:
Any further increase in wheat prices now would aggravate the problems of economic and political readjustment of the liberated areas to Canada's detriment in future trade with those areas. There is a moral obligation not to take advantage of our recent allies in their time of compelling need.
Higher wheat prices would encourage the importing countries in a hurried return to wheat production and pre-war wheat policies very directly to the detriment of the wheat exporting countries, particularly Canada. Moreover, production in a number of exporting countries would be unduly encouraged.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
That was the statement of policy contained in the last three or four paragraphs of the statement read to the house on that occasion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. But what I wish to emphasize particularly is the fact that from the very first statement made in the house it was a five-year period which was discussed.
At a later stage of the discussion in relation to this matter I stated to the house that the period was a five-year period, that the period previously discussed by the government of Canada with the international wheat committee had been a five-year period, but that we had not been able to prevail upon the committee to discuss a period so long, and they had insisted upon the period's being cut down to three years, so far as their discussions were concerned.
But when it came to a matter of discussing prices, we were not able to reach agreement in the international committee as to what the price would be. Canada's submission in that regard was that the minimum price should be $1, and the maximum price should be $1.50, preferably, so far as we are concerned, over the longer period of five years. But the committee was not able to arrive at a decision even with regard to the $1 to S1.50 on a shorter period of three years. When that time was reached, this announcement was made to the house; and it was definitely stated at that time that it was a five-year period which it was desired to arrange for; but that it would be impossible to enter into negotiations immediately, and that when they were entered into it would take some time to carry them through.
So that we were going to put ourselves in a position of safeguarding the farmers for a five-year period by putting the floor of $1 under wheat for that entire period; and we were going to see that for the time being we were prepared to deliver wheat to Great Britain and the other allied countries overseas-it was intended to eliminate the United States and other countries which are exporters of wheat themselves-at $1.55 a bushel.
It was definitely indicated that was only an undertaking given in order to make negotiations possible. As I said a minute ago, negotiations were opened in January, 1946, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce and 1 were in Great Britain. Those negotiations continued until the announcement was made in this house that we had succeeded in agreeing to the contract made a few weeks ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I do not think I need go into details regarding the contract, further than to say that under that contract we have already been
delivering wheat to Great Britain in considerably higher quantities than we had beeD [DOT]accustomed to deliver it to them, and this was done throughout the 1945 crop year which ended on July 31, 1946. Deliveries had been made in very much greater quantities than we had been accustomed to deliver wheat to Great Britain; and we were delivering it at $1.55 a bushel. We were also delivering wheat to other allied countries on a similar rate, and in the meantime carrying on our negotiations.
The contract provides that for the years 1946-47 and 1947-48 the price at which wheat is to be delivered to Great Britain is still to be $1.55. It provides that the quantity for those two years is to be 160 million bushels a year. I think it is important to remember that our average deliveries to Great Britain, for consumption in Great Britain, for a long period prior to the war was 90 million bushels a year.
Was not 102 million bushels the highest?

About that; it averaged 90 million bushels. I have not all the figures here at the present time. But the average was 90 million bushels for a period of years, and in certain years it could have been much shorter or much longer and the figure would not have varied much. Around 90 million bushels was what we sold Great Britain.
I consider it is something of an accomplishment to have 70 million bushels added to that 90 million bushels for a period of four full years. We have delivered more than that to Great Britain during the year we have just come through at the figure of $1.55. So that I say we have this considerable accomplishment for two years of supplying them with 70 million bushels more wheat than we had supplied them in the years preceding the war. We think it is somewhat of an accomplishment to point out that for two years more we are going to be able to supply them with 50 million bushels more than the average amount which Great Britain took from us during the years preceding the war.
In other words, the average for the four years is 60 million bushels more, or 66J per cent more wheat delivered to Great Britain under this contract than we have been accustomed to being able to deliver there for consumption in Great Britain.
There is, of course, the' provision in the contract under which Great Britain may sell or dispose of some of this wheat in the form of either wheat or flour to others. We have placed no restriction upon her in that regard. One can only answer the criticism by saying

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that if Britain is anything like as good a trader as she is accused of being and if she has to pay a higher price for wheat in any other country from which she might purchase at the present time than she is having to pay to Canada, at least during the period when wheat is higher that $1.55 if purchased from other countries Britain is not at all likely to dispose of any considerable part of the 160 or 140 million bushels of wheat to anyone else. In other words, she is buying this wheat in the first instance in order to serve her own people and be assured that food is available for them. If Great Britain finds is necessary to send 10 million bushels to India or even to some country in Europe in order to feed people who would not otherwise be fed, I have no doubt she will probably do that; but as for taking our wheat and selling it in some other countiy in order to make more out of it than they had paid to Canada, I doubt very much if Britain would even consider doing any such thing at any particular time, no matter w-hat the situation is.
What I want to emphasize is that we have assured Canada a sure market for a period of four more years of at least 150 million bushels of wheat on an average for each year during that period. A question which has arisen as a result of the fact that most of our discussions have been of a four year contract in order to complete a five-year period is as to whether there has been any change in the policy which was discussed with the farm organizations and others as to the participation payment on the 1945 crop. I wish to say that all the discussions that have taken place with Great Britain, with the farm organizations, in the wheat committee of council with the wheat board and others, and in the council have been in connection with a five-year period just as was announced on September 19, 1945.
It was not until about a month ago that there was any discussion whatsoever of separating the payments in relation to the 1945 crop from the payments of the last four years of the period. . I am going to indicate how that discussion came about and where it had its origin. It did not have its origin with the farm organizations, and in a moment. I shall state the reason for saying that. In all our discussions with the farm organizations we discussed the possibilities of what might be called a five-year pool. We were to put all of the returns from our wheat into a fund and PaJ' out a certain initial payment. Then at the end of the five-year period we would divide up any profits that were made among the farmers in proportion to the amounts
[Mr. Gardiner. 1
that they had delivered to the pool during that period of time. If there were a loss instead of a profit the government undertook to take that loss after having once set the initial payment.
At the time the discussions started, the initial payment was $1.25, and the main criticism of the proposal made by the government in September, 1945, was that we had substituted $1 for $1.25. We made it very plain that that was not intended to be the price to the farmer, that it was only a safeguard to the farmer for the five-year period until such time as we could negotiate a final agreement with the British to take a very considerable proportion of our wheat. The contract we negotiated was for. four years with a definite return of $1.55 a bushel in the first two years of that four-year period. A considerable part of the crop for 1645 was sold at $1.55, which meant three years of sales at $1.55. There was a guarantee put under the price of SI .25 for the third year of the contract or the fourth year of the pool and $1 for the fifth year of the pool or the fourth year of the contract. It was then obvious to everyone that more than S1.25 a bushel could be paid as. an initial payment.
Then the question under discussion was as to how much could be paid out as an initial payment on that wheat. At the time these discussions began, I put a question directly to the representatives of all the farm organizations which met in the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I asked whether I was right in assuming that in all these discussions we were prepared to undertake a five-year pooling of the returns from the crop. I also asked whether I was right in assuming that the highest floor price that had ever been asked for officially by any farm organization up to that time was $1.25 a bushel. I then recited to them the terms of the contract which had not yet been signed and indicated that we were hopeful we w'ould still have the support of the farm organizations in entering into a contract for four years on the understanding that the floor price would not be less than $1.25 a bushel. The answer I got to all those questions was that what I w'as assuming was the position that had been assumed all through the discussions. What they wanted was security in the form of stability of prices over a period.
Then they said to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to myself, "We want to discuss with you what we think the advance payment ought to be." We agreed to that and the discussion began as to whether it

Supply-Trade and Commerce
should be $1.35 or $1.40. I think I am correct in saying that every farmer in western Canada, including all the representatives of the farmers, would have been better pleased to get $1.40 as an initial payment than he would to get $1.35. I am not going to argue that anyone representing the farmers or any individual farmer would not have argued in favour of the $1.40, but I think I am right in saying that, after a complete discussion had taken place, those who represented the farm interests-'there were, members from Ontario as well as the president and secretary of the farm federation representing people right across Canada-felt justified in believing that the best possible thought would be given to the whole question and, whether or not they could agree on everything that was decided upon, an effort was being made to give that stabilized return to the farmer at as high as possible a level and over as long a period of time 'as possible. The discussions were then carried on without any further direct negotiations with the farm organizations.
The government gave the fullest possible consideration to the matter. During those considerations the suggestion was made, not by the farm organizations but by an official of the government-this was not a member of the government-that we might consider the possibility of paying out immediately the entire participation payment on the 1945 crop and then, after having done that, determine upon the lower rate of $1.35 a bushel to the farmer for the four-year period. That matter was discussed indirectly with farm organizations, not in a meeting of them all together but indirectly with those who represent farm organizations. I think I would be correct in saying that that would have been preferable to what has been suggested. It was considered preferable on the ground that a very high participation payment was assumed as going to be made for the 1945 crop. That is where the question comes in that was raised a few moments ago by the minister. That very high initial payment was figured on this basis, that if you take all the wheat which was supplied to the Canadian people for consumption at $1.25 a bushel out of the 1944 crop, the participation payment on the 1944 crop would be relatively low and the participation payment on 1945 would be relatively high. When it was known that figures which had been used in the discussion involved that consideration the question naturally suggested itself whether or not that was the just thing to do; and we came to the conclusion, right or wrong, that it was not the just thing to do. That was between the time the announcement was

made by the minister of the sixteen cents advance for 1944 and the announcement he made to-day.
The position to-day is this. When the proportion of the wheat that was utilized in 1944 for supplying the mills in Canada is charged up to the pool of 1944 and the proportion that was utilized in 1945 is charged up to the 1945 crop, the participation payment for 1944 will go up and the participation payment for 1945 will go down by a relative figure. The only cost that would have been against the 1945 crop under the previous suggestion would have been the cost of handling, and the handling cost was very low in 1945 because wheat was coming out of the elevators faster than it was going in, because we got rid of all our surplus that had been carried over from other years as well as all the crop for that year. So that there has been very little charged up against that wheat during 1945 and 1946. When that adjustment is made the question is not as important to the farmers as if the payment had been made the other way.
As a result of what we have done, namely, establishing an initial payment of $1.35, the participation payments are immediately being made on the 1943 crop; they are being made now. I think it would be the duty of the wheat board, as soon as possible after that, to pay the additional ten cents a bushel out of the 1945 crop, which would bring the initial payment for that whole five-year period up to $1.35 instead of $1.25. That ten cents will be paid out on the 1945 crop. I say that in order to emphasize the fact that while the different way of figuring it, which I think is the just and proper way, reduces the amount of participation for 1945 at the top by an amount which I do not yet know, it reduces the amount by ten cents at the bottom, and there is not so much in between to be considered at the moment when we are talking about whether participation payments should be immediately paid out on the 1945 crop as separate from the crops of the other four years.
The position then is this, that we have decided that the policy ought to be to make an initial payment for the whole five years of $1.35, and any earnings that are made on the crop should be charged up to participation. If there are any losses taken as we go along through the programme those will be charged up against the same fund, and this year's participation will be paid out at the end of the season.
Some may ask why we should ask the farmers to wait so long? I would submit that the most important reason is that if we are

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to have long-term contracts that stabilize prices we must be prepared to do what everyone has suggested we should be prepared to do. I agree with those who say that we should not be asked to do more, only to the extent that we are asking some other people to do certain things.
It is not right to say that the people of Canada have never been asked to assume any losses in connection with wheat and thus help the farmer, because in one year in handling wheat under the wheat board we lost $61,000,000, and that was taken out of the treasury of Canada or charged up to all the people of Canada and paid.
What year was that?

On the 1938-39 crop.
In some other years we lost a lesser amount. Under the arrangements which we have, carried on since 1935, we have always undertaken that the treasury of Canada would take all the losses and that the farmers of Canada who grow the wheat would get all the profits. Perhaps we are being just a little too critical as western farmers when we say that we should be insistent that no part of the advantage which is gained by keeping down the costs of living through keeping down the cost of the loaf of bread should be charged up to the farmer alone. The amount that should be charged up should be limited as much as possible, but I think we shall all agree that there is some justification for our taking some of the chances.
Having said that, may I say that farm organizations generally, the farmers in particular, and most of us who represent wheatgrowing constituencies in this house have always questioned the advisability of charging the farmer up with the difference between whatever the price was and the price at which wheat was being supplied to the millers. In other words, it, should be emphasized over and over against that every banker, every operator, every railroad, every clerk in a bank or store, every labourer, every farmer has been buying flour, or his bread to put it in other terms, on the basis of 78-cents wheat ever since control came into effect in this country. In other words, we have been supplying that important food product to the people of this country, to the labouring people and consumers generally, at a lower rate than it is supplied anywhere else in the world. I agree with those who say that that whole cost should not be charged up to the farmer, and in discussions in the past I have maintained that too much of that cost has been charged up fMr. Gardiner.]
to the farmer. I still maintain that we should get away from that just as soon as we possibly can.
Having said that, may I revert to what I said a few moments ago. The argument is not all on one side. The treasury has paid the losses on our wheat before; it may have to pay losses again, and those losses if paid will be paid to the same farmers against whom this cost was charged up. That is the position at the moment.
In the discussions that have taken place the question was raised whether the floor price should be for this whole five-year period. You can carry right on through the season and apply any argument you like with regard to it, but these are all the facts which are available in this connection.
Finally, instead of adopting either one or the other alternative, we did adhere to the $1.35 as the initial payment, and we said that the final payment would be made at the end of the five years on that basis. But it is not correct to say that there will be no participation payment from now until the end of the five years. We are just in the midst of making the 1943 payment, and then we must pay out the ten cents a bushel on the 1945 crop, which will take some time. I hope it will not take so long as it took to get around to the 1943 payment, but it will take some time. Then we shall have to pay out on 1944; it will be a substantial payment, and it will have to be refigured in the light of some of the things I have said in the last few moments. In other words, I shall be very much surprised if we are able to complete those payments earlier than the end of 1947; and I would be very much surprised too, in the light of some things I have heard here to-day, if the farmers would want it all paid within that period of time. We hear a lot of things said about income tax; and I am not so sure, if anybody is right in arguing, as many have argued in this house and outside, that we are taking a big risk in the last years of this contract, but that some who are worrying about the contract would rather have the payment made toward the end rather than the beginning. The treasury would like to have it paid out in the beginning and maybe are urging the chairman of the wheat board to pay it out early. But some of the farmers will say, "As long as we know we are going to get it we shall be fairly well satisfied." So that, after all, the only time the farmers have to wait without any participation is, at the outside, two years. They may not have to wait that long; they may be getting annual

Supply-Trade and Commerce
payments for two years or two and a half years and then have to wait the remainder of the period in order to get their final payments on the five-year pool. I do not think that is an objectionable arrangement in so far as the farmer is -concerned. I am going to say this, and to say it after having had one experience of saying a similar thing before and resolving never to say it again. I said I had no complaints about certain things which had been done. Then the next day somebody proceeded to organize complaints and I got a considerable number of them. But I am going to say this: I have just completed a trip in western Canada. I addressed a meeting in Edmonton of eight thousand people, most of them farmers; and about a month earlier I addressed a meeting at Kenosee park, southern Saskatchewan, where I gave them the terms of the agreement. I addressed another meeting at Battleford and did the same thing. I spent the great part of three days in the first week of August at the Regina fair, meeting farmers every day in the barns and around the grounds and elsewhere. Then I attended a Liberal convention-
They were not satisfied?
-at which all of the different corners of Saskatchewan were represented.
"Corners" is right.
As a matter of fact the vote was 623 out of a possible 650, or something like that. They were mostly farmers. I would say that some day again most of the farmers in Saskatchewan will be Liberal.
What a hope!
"Hope springs eternal."

I was at all these gatherings; and I must say this, that not a single person, farmer or otherwise, raised a complaint in regard to this agreement. They did not all mention it; but all who did mention it spoke of it in very glowing terms and said, "It is the thing we have been waiting for in this country ever since we have been here, to know, three or four years in advance, what we are going to get for our crop, and know at the same time that the return is a reasonable one."
This morning I went over the records to satisfy myself on what has been happening in relation to wheat and to compare it with what is proposed under this agreement. I find that the time of highest returns for any five-year period in the history of wheat-growing in western Canada was the five years around
the end of the last war, from 1916-17 to 1920-21. The average price over that period for No. 1 northern at Fort William was $2.22 a bushel. That was a period of government control of the marketing of wheat. It was the period when we had our first experiences with the wheat board. It was the period when wheat was being marketed from government to government, and during that time we had an average return of $2.22 a bushel basis No. 1 northern at Fort William for all the wheat marketed. On August 15, 1920, or, in other words, at the beginning of the 1920-21 crop it was decided to throw the market open and discontinue control. Wheat remained above $2 for four months. Hon. members remember that wheat had averaged $2.22 in all the previous five-year period; it was up at around $2.50 or S2.60 when controls were taken off, and it remained above $2 for four months. In the fifth month it went below $2 and continued constantly downward, to ninety-three cents a bushel in December of 1923. Every member of this house from western Canada knows it was as a result of that experience that the pools were organized in western Canada in 1923-24. I remember an experience which I had between that period which I have never forgotten and never will forget. I went dowm to borrow $600 on a carload of wheat. The banker said to me, "I should not lend you this". I said, "Why not?" He said, "I have got instructions from head office not to lend any money on wheat being held." But he wrote out the note and pushed it across the table; I signed the note, got the $600. and spent it. Well, I was not able to pay back the bank until I sold my next year's crop. I lost just exactly the $600 on the carload of wheat, selling it the next spring after this drop in price which I have just indicated to the committee. Every farmer in western Canada who grew wheat there from 1920 to 1923-24 had that experience. There is no reason why anyone should be surprised in going to western Canada to-day to hear every western farmer say, "I am prepared to see this thing tried out; it is better than anything that has been proposed to us before. We expect more from it; we are going to support it". They all had a similar experience; people sitting on the other side of the house had it; they can remember it just as well as I can.

We made our speeches
eighteen years sooner, though.
No; I made mine and they were heard at that time by more people than heard my hon. friend.

The same thing will happen again.

Twenty-two million.

Twenty-two million in the final result. Before it was settled it was somewhere around $30 million. Some of that amount was picked up afterwards, but the final figure of $22 million and some odd dollars had to be taken care of by other arrangements made by governments. Those of us who w,ere in government were there at the time and had to take part in the negotiations which resulted in the settlement. As a result of that, other kinds of control were tried for a while, and finally the market was thrown open. During the period of thirteen years from the time the contract pools went out to 1843 when government control was again put on, the average price received for wheat was eighty-two cents a bushel. I am not going to say that that was all due to there being open markets. I know it was not. There were world conditions which have been dis-

cussed here many times that helped to bring about the result. The fact remains that during those thirteen years the average price was eighty-two cents a bushel; and over the twenty-three years from 1920-21 to 1943, the average price was SI .07 a bushel, even including the average of $1.47 over the five years of the pooling period. All I say to hon. members is that when we are discussing this question we ought to take past experience into consideration. I know of no period except the two periods in which we had some kind of control, the one put on by the government itself and the other by the cooperative farm organizations, when wheat ever remained above the $1.45 a bushel for five years. Therefore, cn that basis we concluded that SI .35 was a reasonable position to start from, and that we could start from it only with a contract signed with the British government to take an average of 150 million bushels of wheat over a four-year period at a price which gave us a good sum to begin with. Starting from there, we believe that we can market sufficient wheat in other places at similar returns or higher for the earlier part of the period, and if we necessarily must, at lower returns in the latter part of the period and thus bring it to $1.35 paid to farmers, with little if any loss to Canada.
I must say that the objection taken with regard to flour made in Canada and delivered to our own people is that it may result in some losses to the farmers themselves; but toward the end of this period there may be losses taken on the other side by all the people of Canada who are the consumers of flour, and until we get to the end of the period we cannot be absolutely certain as to whether our criticism is just or not. Mj^ understanding is that the $1.25 is intended to be retained only until such time as controls are released in certain directions to such an extent as to make it possible to release this one also. It is not a part of the whole five-year programme. It may be that after three months, six months or a year that may happen. I am not in a position to state how long it will be on, but it is not part of a programme which continues right throughout the whole five-year period.
These are the chief points that I want to bring out in connection with the contract that has been presented. There is only one other point that I should like to make, namely, that we believe that stability of price is more valuable to farmers under present conditions than the opportunity to get a higher return at present, with chances that we are going to have to take a much lower return at a period a little later on. I think I have the agree-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ment of most hon. members on both sides of the committee that it will be a good thing for agriculture, in western Canada particularly, and in all of Canada, if we can establish that stability for farm returns across the country.
It would be better for all Canada; we shall all prosper together.

Yes. We have contracts for pork; we have contracts for cheese; we have contracts for butter; we have contracts for milk; and they are all on the same basis for a long period of time at a stabilized price. Wheat and beef are the only two left. While I am discussing the wheat contract which has just been completed, I wish to say that a beef contract is under negotiation. I think the final touches will be put to it while I am over in England during the next week or two. When we have it prepared we shall be able to bring it back here and announce it. We hope to have all farm prices put on a basis where we can try to stabilize the return for farm products over a period of from three to five years.
What I wanted to say is that we are going to have criticism. We are going to have people telling us that we can sell our wheat for a great deal more in certain places. I have heard the argument raised here that wheat can be sold in the United States for SI.87 a bushel. As a matter of fact the illustration put out in advertising across the country was that on the street in Portal, North Dakota, wheat was selling at $1.87 a bushel, and that wheat at the boundary, which is only an imaginary line running between the two towns, on the street in Portal was $1.07 a bushel, Canadian funds. I wish to state that neither of these statements is correct.
Did the minister say $1.07?

At North Portal, and
$1.87 at Portal, or a difference of eighty cents between the two. Anyone reading any of these advertisements would come to the conclusion that a Canadian farmer could take a load of wheat from North Portal, cross the boundary to Portal and get $1.87 a bushel for it in Canadian funds, but if he delivered it to an elevator on the north side of the line he would get only $1.07. In the first place, if you could deliver wheat into the United States at all at any price you would have to pay forty-two cents a bushel duty on it in order to get it across the boundary line at any point. So that, now that our money is at par, you can immediately take forty-two cents off the top end of it. That brings you down to a difference of thirty-eight cents, not
eighty cents. Then, starting at the other end, $1.07 is not the street price of wheat anywhere in western Canada. The $1.07 a bushel represents the difference of eighteen cents between $1.25 at Fort William and the advance made on wheat at North Portal; and with the ten cents we are going to pay now as a result of this price of $1.35 and anything paid on top of that at the end of the period under this arrangement, as a result of the final participation, deducted from the bottom end of it- and that may turn to be some six or seven cents-well, you would have only four or five cents left as the difference between the American return and the Canadian return, or the return a Canadian can get for wheat delivered in the United States. It is not eighty cents. When anyone takes 200,000,000 bushels of wheat and multiplies it by eighty cents and says the farmers have lost that much money, well, the farmers of western Canada are not foolish enough to believe that. They know it is not true, and of course that kind of figuring does not get anyone anywhere.
I wanted to say that much with respect to that matter, but you cannot sell a bushel of wheat in the United States at any price.
Nonsense.

Well, perhaps it is nonsense to say you cannot sell a bushel at any time. Under the arrangement that now exists and that was established by the United States government, not by us, there is an embargo on every bushel of wheat going into that country beyond 800,000 bushels; and that has been the case during almost the entire war period. That is not aimed at anyone but Canada. No other country exports or could export any considerable quantity of wheat to the United States. For milling purposes you cannot send into the United States more than 800,000 bushels of wheat in a year, and that amount goes into that country in the first forty-eight hours of the period, or if not in the first forty-eight hours, certainly within the first week. So that our farmers are not in a position to sell wheat in the United States at all, and why hold up before us this offer of $1.87 a bushel for wheat in that country when we cannot sell wheat there?
It has been said in the newspapers and elsewhere that the American people have been criticizing our agreement with Great Britain. I do not care who may say that, I think I know the American people well enough to know that no considerable number are doing any such thing. They have retained their home market for themselves, and that is their own business. They are paying their own

Supply-Trade and Commerce
people $1.87 a bushel for wheat, and they are not paying the Canadian farmer that price. Since we cannot market our wheat in the United States, we must find a market for it somewhere else. Since they are retaining their own home market, I do not know of any other place in the world where we can sell 160,000,000 bushels of wheat, except in Great Britain. We sold the United States approximately 160,000,000 bushels of wheat one year during the war, as feed for their live stock, even when they had an embargo against anything beyond 800,000 bushels to be milled into flour for consumption in that country. We sold them that wheat so that they could produce live stock and get more meat for the American people. I do not believe any considerable number of people in the United States, in the government or outside it, have raised any criticism of this government going to Great Britain and making an agreement on this basis. But somebody says, "oh, you have made a bilateral agreement and they do not like that." Well, for the life of me I cannot see why the grain exchange or anyone interested in the grain exchange would prefer to have multilateral agreements instead of bilateral agreements. If a bilateral agreement made by the government will tend to close the grain exchange in Canada, surely a multilateral agreement throughout the world will close all the grain exchanges in the world; so why should anyone associated with the grain trade want that? I do not know why, but the advertisements which have appeared would indicate that what they are really against is bilateral trading. Well, I hope I am not looked upon as an impossible imperialist, but I am enough of an imperialist to believe that there is no place in the world where Canada will be better treated than within the British empire.
I am quite satisfied to be partly responsible for entering into an agreement w'ith Britain under which they agree to do a thing which will be beneficial to us, and under which we agree to do a thing which will be beneficial to them. Unless we can negotiate arrangements of that kind, bilateral or multilateral, we shall have difficulties in the world that nothing will solve short of another war such as the one we have just come through.
Why don't you come over here?

What I should say to my hon, friend is, why didn't you stay where you were? The trouble with those hon. gentlemen over there was that they were just Liberals in a hurry. They were, I think, in a hurry to get into this house more than anything else. They are here now and talking 
good Liberal doctrine. I am glad to hear them talking it, because it does not in any way hurt the position of Liberalism elsewhere.
Some of us could have been here a long time ago had we chosen to come another way.
Well, that reminds me that the other day my hon. friend said he would not become leader of the Liberal party. I would suggest that he might wait until he is asked.
That is exactly it; I said I had not been officially asked.

That is a very good
reason for not discussing it at all.
Exactly. I would have been the last one to raise it.

The best reason I know for anyone not wanting to become the leader of any party is that he has not been asked. That is sufficient, without anything further.
The position with regard to this whole matter is that we are able to sell a sufficient amount of our wheat in a sure market, at sure pay, to warrant us in agreeing to stabilize the initial payment for five years at $1.35 a bushel; then undertaking to attempt in that period of time to make still further earnings for the farmer and pay those out at the end. Again I submit that this policy is one that appeals to farmers in western Canada generally. When we are at the end of the four-3-ear period, if in the last six or twelve months we find ourselves in the position that world markets, so-called, are not offering as much for wheat as we are getting for it, I hope people will still stand behind us to the extent they are standing behind us now. Even if wheat stays above $1.55 during the whole period, I hope people will still feel that it was worth while trying. If we are successful ip this experiment, then we can talk to the grain trade people with some assurance. If they are able to show us at the end of the five-year period that we were all wrong, that oyer that length of time the farmer got less than he ever got before under similar circumstances and that the other system would have brought him more, then we shall be in a position to discuss the matter with them on an even footing. I am sure anyone who has taken this position and finds himself wrong will be quite prepared to discuss it from that point of view. In the meantime we are convinced that this is the best thing for the farmer. As long as we are convinced of that, and having another four years in which to try it out, we can put the policy into effect in a way that will at least help us to determine how this
