long argument between farmer and grain trade in western Canada ought to be settled in the interests of the great masses of the people.

Mr. Chairman, the item before the committee is one in the wheat and grain division of the Department of Trade and Commerce, in which an amount of $28,000 is being asked. At the beginning of the discussion on it the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a brief comment with respect to the United Kingdom wheat agreement, and the government wheat policy which he had formerly outlined to the house. To-day the Minister of Agriculture has given us the background of the discussions leading up to the United Kingdom wheat agreement, and has supported that agreement with such arguments as he was able to bring forward.
I rise at this time to criticize the government's wheat policy. But before doing so, let me say this, with respect to the United Kingdom wheat agreement. Any agreement such as this which tends to level out the inequalities, and the wide fluctuation of prices in the past, is a step in the right direction. Even this agreement is better than no agreement at all; because, as the Minister of Agriculture pointed out, those of us who went through the price depression following the last war know the danger of proceeding without some kind of plan to try to avoid wide fluctuations in price.	"
Having said this, I wish now to point out some of the weaknesses in the arrangement, as [ see them. Briefly, what is the government's wheat policy? It is, .first, that the initial payment for wheat for a five-year period, including this year, will be $1.35. In that period of time are four j'ears in the future, and one which has passed.
The second point is that wheat deliveries shall not be restricted for this year, but that in each of the later years they may be restricted. In other words something less than the whole crop may be taken by the government.
The minimum is fourteen bushels to the acre.

The third point is that the wheat board may sell farmers' wheat in three different ways and at three different prices. It may sell domestic wheat at $1.25; it may sell to the United Kingdom under this agreement for two years at $1.55. and for two years at an undetermined price. The minimum in one of those years is $1.25. and in the last year it is SI. The remainder of any wheat not so sold may be sold at world prices, now in the neighbourhood of $2 a bushel. So far as price is concerned, that is the substance
of the arrangement. As the minister has said, in the first two years the United Kingdom will take 160 million bushels instead of 90 million or 100 million, the average amount taken before the war. In the later two years it will take 140 million bushels.
I shall not make the numerous detailed criticisms of this policy one could make. My major criticisms are these: First, that the price of SI.35, the initial payment, is less than a fair price. It is less than a parity price for wheat. A parity price for wheat to-day would be in the neighbourhood of $1.50. It will be noted that $1.35 is ten per cent less than that.
It may be urged that this is an initial payment, but there is no assurance that farmers will receive any more than that. To the extent that there is no such assurance, the wheat growers in this country and other farmers as well will not be assured of a fair relationship of their prices to their costs of production. That is my first criticism of the agreement. At a time when the world price is much higher than parity it does not assure to farmers even parity. I ask the committee this question: If we cannot have parity now, what hope is there for parity when the world market situation is reversed, and the price is low?
In this connection I would point out that in the years 1939, 1940, 1941 and 1942 farmers of Canada sold their wheat at prices thirty to forty cents below parity. It is only in the last two or three years that the price has equalled, or slightly exceeded what has been spoken of as parity, or a figure reached by economists which is supposed to represent a fair relationship between the prices farmers receive and the cost of things they have to buy.
My second criticism is that the guarantee of $1.35 a bushel is in many respects an empty guarantee. After this year, there is no guarantee that the government will allow the full crop to be sold. There is no guarantee that it will allow more than fourteen bushels to the acre to be sold. There is no guarantee that they will take more than fourteen bushels to the acre on more than two-thirds of the acreage sown in 1940.
In those respects, as I said, this guarantee is an empty one. To the extent that it is a guarantee of $1.35 a bushel on fourteen bushels to the acre, on a reduced acreage, it is a guarantee. But it is not a guarantee of $1.35 on all the crop grown on all the acres which may be producing in Canada in the next five years.
The third criticism, one which was advanced earlier by another hon. member, is that the government's policy is to hold back the pay-
Supply-Trade and Commerce

ment of participation certificates until the end the five-year period. The Minister of Agriculture has intimated that in the next 3'ear or two there will be some participation certificates for back years which will be made. That is true. But it is a new feature of government policy to state that under this so-called five-year plan any money which may be due to farmers will be held back until the plan is completed, instead of being paid as soon as the product of each year is sold, and the- costs and receipts computed.
I have sometimes wondered why the government brought forward a policy with the last-mentioned weakness in it. I can see no other reason than their fear that in the later years of the agreement the price will be low and what may be held back by the government now can be used to supplement the price then.
My fourth criticism is this: The guarantee is spoken of as a price guarantee. In so far as it goes it is all right, but a price guarantee is not an income guarantee, nor is a price guarantee a purchasing power guarantee. As I have already said, the price guarantee on a part of the production from each acre and on a reduced acreage is not a price guarantee on all that is produced.
I think it was desirable that there be an approach made to a sale of this kind to the United Kingdom, but I do not think this was a good bargain on Canada's part. I think it was a bad bargain. I think it will create a handicap in the development of future markets in other places. In some respects I think it is an improvident arrangement. I think it will tend to restrict the expansion of Canada's trade rather than to expand Canada's world trade. I think, in making this arrangement, the government has backed away from its commitments of the past with respect to the widening of Canadian trade.
Before I proceed further, let me deal with one or two matters mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture just before he sat down. He referred to the fact that somebody had said that wheat was sold at a Canadian border point for $1.07 and that wheat had been sold for $1.87 in the United States. I do not know what impression the minister sought to leave by making that statement; but, lest there be some question as to what the so-called world price is, I should like to read from a document of Canada's own wheat board, circular No. 23, dated July 30, 1946. I shall not read it all; but section B, clause 2, which refers to a number of countries to which flour shipments may be made, reads as follows:

The price governing sales to the above countries will be basis our current class 2 price which, at this date, is $2.05 per bushel basis one northern, in store, Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver.
We thus have what is in effect a four-price system in Canada. There is the price of seventy-eight to millers for the production of flour for home use; there is the price of $1.25 on wheat used for certain domestic purposes; there is the price of $1.55 to Britain; and there is the price they can get in other markets, they are trying now to get $2.05. That is the wheat price structure as we have it now in Canada.
Let me refer now to another point made by the Minister of Agriculture. He said that this agreement would bring about something more in the way of stability of prices, and that it was a five-year arrangement. A little later I shall touch upon the five-year feature- show that one year has already passed and that in the last two years of the arrangement the agreement means practically nothing so far as price is concerned, that in its main features this agreement is not much more than a two-year agreement. The minister said that it was made for the purpose of bringing about stability in agriculture. I say that in some respects it is an improvident arrangement. In this connection I should like to read what a newspaper which has always been a great friend of this government has to say about some of the aspects of this arrangement. I shall not read all the editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of August 5, 1946, but I will try to sort out the pertinent parts. The editorial reads:
The Canadian government is trying to defend the bad bargain it has made in its wheat contract with the United Kingdom by exploiting a prejudice which has no relation to the facts.
Running right through the statements of those who seek to justify this agreement is the assumption that the only alternative to a contract is the danger that wheat prices, some years from now, will fall to the low levels of the depression.
Mr. MacKinnon, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has said, for example, that the contract protects western farmers "from crippling losses should there be a world slump in wheat prices."
Now, nobody should know better than Mr. MacKinnon that it is not necessary to have a wheat contract in order to shield farmers from depression prices. He himself has brought in an alternative policy which tries to do this very thing. All he is doing, in sponsoring the new contract, is repudiating his own previous handiwork.
Speaking in the House of Commons on September 19, 1945, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. MacKinnon, said-
I do not know whether this is the occasion to which the Minister of Agriculture referred.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The same occasion.

These are the minister's words:
"The government recognizes the paramount need for relative stability of income to wheat producers. Toward this end, the government undertakes that in the five-year period ending July 31, 1950, producers will receive not less than $1 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver on the authorized deliveries for each crop year. By providing a long-term floor price of not less than $1, the government will protect producers against the consequences of any sharp reversal in the world wheat position during the next five-year period."
In short, our wheat industry is not faced by any panic conditions. The policy now abandoned by Mr. MacKinnon and the government was, in reality, designed to safeguard the farmer against the "crippling losses" which, it is now claimed, can only be prevented by the United Kingdom contract and similar bilateral arrangements.
Without reading all the editorial, let me quote from another part which reads:
It should be emphasized, above all else, that there really is no guarantee that Canadian farmers will receive not less than $1.25 per bushel of wheat in the third year of this bilateral deal and not less than $1 for the fourth year, as the contract now stipulates. The contract is full of so many obscurities and escape clauses that these prices, in practice, may be made subject to further discussion and negotiation in the light of world conditions as they will exist at that time. They are far from being an irrevocable commitment by the United Kingdom.
The British government is much too good a trader to pay Canada more than the world price.
Yet that is what the government is counting on in the later years of this agreement.
Under a contract.

The editorial continues:
Of course, it-that is the British Government -is quite agreeable to paying us about 50 cents less per bushel than the world price, if we accept such a policy and fix it in a contract.
And that is what the government has done.
Besides, it will always be within Britain's power to take suitable reprisals against us if we try to enforce the letter of the contract against her wishes or her needs. This is a pretty flimsy sort of guarantee for stability of income to the Canadian wheat producer.
We cannot take refuge in the contract and hope to escape the world price.
What the editorial is trying to say is, how can Britain in the later years of this arrangement, if the price of wheat is low, pay to Canada more than the world price? It goes on:
The contract, in short, simply obliges us to sell Britain more wheat than she normally takes from Canada for her own use, and to do so at a figure far below the current world price. We then give her a contractual right to sell the
balance at any price she can get and to keep this profit for herself, even though it is made exclusively out of our wheat.
The editorial ends this way:
This is surely an incompetent way for the Canadian government to try to run the farmers' business.
What we are saying to the greatest wheat importer in the world at a time when the price of wheat is high is this: We will sell our wheat to you at about fifty cents a bushel less than the world price in the hope that some time later on when the price is low you will remember and make up for this generosity on our part. I put the question to this committee, would you if you were members of a British parliament, if the price of wheat should go down to a $1 a bushel, would you ask the workingmen of Britain to pay $1.55 a bushel for wheat? And if you did ask that, would they let you pay it? It is not a question of their wanting to break any contract. It is a question of their not being able to come through. And it will be noticed that they have not agreed to come through. Any practical man will say that there is no prospect that they will pay us more later on than the world price, low as it may be.
I have said this arrangement was a bad bargain, and I want again to refer to this paper-a prominent organ of public opinion- which is sometimes right and which I think on this matter is right. Here is what it has to say on August 1:	.
The wheat agreement is a bargain. Canada agrees to sell; the United Kingdom agrees to buy. How does the bargain work out?
I shall not take time to have you follow the logic of their reasoning, but I will read the pertinent parts of their argument:
Mr. MacKinnon would leave the matter there. But he fails to note another and considerable advantage which accrues to the United Kingdom. Under the agreement . . . Canada undertakes to provide more wheat, particularly in the first two years-the period of the expected scarcity- than the United Kingdom normally receives from this country.
Britain agrees to take 160 million bushels of our wheat where normally she used to take from 90 to 100 million bushels. The editorial goes on:
Moreover, the agreement contemplates the sale at the contract price of quantities of wheat beyond those stipulated.
What is the United Kingdom going to do with the excess of Canadian wheat thus bought from Canada at a fire-sale price? The point has substance, was foreseen by the two governments, and is specifically covered in the agreement by clause 3, "it is agreed that the United Kingdom
government may sell or dispose of the wheat and our purchased under this agreement in whatsoever manner the United Kingdom government may deem expedient both in regard to destination and price."

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Britain in the past has taken only 90 to 100 million bushels of our wheat; she has now agreed to take 160 million bushels a year at fifty cents below the world price, and she can sell the surplus where she pleases at whatever price she can get. The editorial goes on:
In a word, Canada not only undertakes to meet Britain's normal requirements of Canadian wheat at a heavy loss in price. Canada goes further and presents the United Kingdom with quantities of wheat which the United Kingdom is free, under the contract, to sell at the world price, keeping the profit. Canada says:	Here
is the wheat you normally need from us at 45 cents per bushel less than it is worth. And here is more wheat which, if you care to do so, you can sell at a good profit. We do not want this money. You keep it and remember, two years hence, how generous we have been.
It goes on:
From the standpoint of this country retaining its own place in the wheat trade of the world, the folly of this course is clear. Here, however, we are only concerned with how the bargain will work out. Additional to the advantages of being able to buy her normal supplies of Canadian whe*at for much less than it is presently worth, the United Kingdom is being set up as a seller of Canadian wheat. The wheat thus sold will be Canada's wheat. The customers who buy it will be customers of the United Kingdom. The profit which results will be Britain's profit.
It will^be observed in all the comment in the United Kingdom on the agreement that while great emphasis is placed on the fact that Canadian wheat is now to be bought for less than it is worth, no mention is made of paying more than it is worth later on.
One comment from London reads: "The Canadian price is lower than the United States' or Argentine prices to-day and if Canada is willing to promise deliveries at that price for the next two years it would be a foolish buyer who would refuse." "Foolish" is the right word. Another comment runs: "For Britain this represents an enormous bargain at 5 shillings and 7 pence per bushel while the current price of Canadian wheat is 8 shillings per bushel." Again, the phrase "an enormous bargain" is strictly accurate.
There is a large question mark against the advantage which Canada hopes to receive. It remains to be seen if the United Kingdom will pay a penny over the market price two years hence. There is nothing binding in the agreement and all experience is against any such assumption.
Therefore, the agreement is one-sided. Canada agrees to make a gift to the consumers of the United Kingdom of 45 cents per bushel on the basis of present prices and, further, to set the United Kingdom up in the wheat business at the expense of our wheat growers. If the world price slumps ,the agreement will not stand, and there is no way in which Canada can make it stand. The disadvantages are real. The advantages are illusory. There is no doubt of the desire of the government to do the right thing, but there is more than doubt of its competence in a business matter of this kind.
I have said that a bilateral policy of this kind is a handicap to our future markets. The minister made light of that description of the arrangement, but, as I shall show later on,

that criticism of bilateral arrangements has been a basic policy of the Liberal party with respect to trade policies. The Winnipeg Free Press, in its issue of August 1, has this to say with respect to that handicap to our future trade:
If the wheat agreement w'ere a snug little deal conferring advantages on the United Kingdom and Canada even though to the disadvantage of other countries, it might be possible to plead immediate justification. In the long run it is true it would work against both signatories but in the short run it might well be attractive.
The present wheat agreement, however, cannot even make as good a showing as this. It is a bad bargain for Canada. By practical everyday standards of business it will not bear scrutiny. And no wizardry in analysis is needed to demonstrate its weaknesses.
Canada's wheat problem is a selling problem. We require all the markets we can find and the largest attainable number of buyers. Therein, lies security for our wheat farmers. And it follows that the most obvious course to avoid is to restrict our markets, to place our eggs largely in one basket.
The editorial ends this way:
The consequence of this will be that at the end of the four years covered by the agreement we will be less able to market our wheat than before the war. We will have lost valuable customers. We will have placed the future of our wheat farmers predominantly in the hands of a single buyer._ There could be no greater insecurity than this. And no agreement which involves such risk to this country and its wheat farmers should have been entered into.
I said also in criticism of the government's arrangement that a contract of this kind will restrict Canada's ability to widen her markets in the future. In other words, it will tend to block the expansion of our exports, the very thing that in so many speeches in this house, from all sides, everybody is trying to bring about-an expansion of exports and an expansion at the same time of imports.
This is what the Winnipeg Free Press has to say in this respect:
It has been stated here, in previous discussions of the -wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, that if the Canadian government prejudiced world trade prospects, now so hopeful, by such a bilateral deal, it would be little less than treason to our international obligations. That treason has now been committed.
By initiating this deal, Canada has violated the spirit and letter of many obligations w-hieh she freely assumed. Canada is pledged, by a series of commitments dating back to the early years of the war, to join in the movement to build a world economy based upon the principles of multilateral trade. That duty is now forgotten. It has been dishonoured by a bilateral deal that will stir up great mischief, and injure the long-term interests of Canada, which cannot prosper except in a -world free from arbitrary trade restrictions.
And it goes on:
The effect of this bilateral agreement will be particularly unhappy in the United States. For some time now, the United States has been

taking the lead in the campaign to liberate world trade. She has reversed the position she assumed after the first world war. Instead of building high tariff walls, she now seeks to reduce or eliminate all discriminatory practices that stifle the growth of trade. In a world burdened with many problems, this American initiative has brought the hope that international cooperation may prove a reality rather than a dream, and that the basis of prosperity may be laid in the vigorous expansion of world trade.
It is difficult to see how Canada's action in the wheat agreement can be fitted into these larger plans. It is an open secret that the United States regards the wheat deal as a contravention of the proposals to be discussed at the world trade conference, preparations for which are now being made in Washington, London and Ottawa, as well as in the capitals of other leading trading nations . . .
On the narrowest possible ground, it is impossible to solve our wheat problem by any such bargain with the United Kingdom as is now contemplated. Before the war Britain took less than 100 million bushels of wheat from Canada; usually the figure was closer to 90 millions. But we had to find a market in the rest of the world for about 150,000,000 or 160,000,000 bushels each year.
There is no security for the farmer in having the contract promise him the sale of 160 million bushels of wheat annually in the British market for the next two crop years and 140 million bushels in each of the last two years of the contract. Great Britain will simply sell the surplus to other countries, thereby making it all the harder for us to market our wheat . . .
The movement to liberate trade was only beginning when the war came. And undoubtedly one of the most hopeful glints of silver in the dark clouds of war has been the belief that the world had learned its lesson and would seize the opportunity which victory would bring to liberate trade.
Listen to this:
This was the promise of the Atlantic charter, of lend-lease, of the united nations charter, of the monetary fund, the world bank, the foreign loans granted by the United States and Canada, the food and agriculture organization, and of the proposed international trade organization. The rebuilding of trade, next to keeping the peace, of which it is an indispensable buttress, has been the greatest promise of these days . . . There is no security for the Canadian farmer in anything but a multilateral trading world.
And the editorial ends in this way:
Thus, in signing the wheat agreement, Canada, the country above all others which depends for prosperity on foreign trade and therefore should be exerting every effort to attaining the freest possible exchange of all goods, has, instead, given the lead backwards to bilateralism and pre-war protectionism.
That is from the newspaper from which I have been quoting up to now.
What paper is that?
The Winnipeg Free Press.

I do not want to hurt anybody's feelings.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: QUERO BANK AREA OFF NOVA SCOTIA-REPORTED DESTRUCTION OF CANADIAN GEAR-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FISHERIES
speechtext: I understand that the Minister of Fisheries, with the indulgence of the house, wants to make a statement to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
subsubtopic: QUERO BANK AREA OFF NOVA SCOTIA-REPORTED DESTRUCTION OF CANADIAN GEAR-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
With the unanimous consent of the house I should like to make the following
statement:
As hon. members know, there have been some complaints in recent weeks that foreign fishing trawlers have destroyed gear set by Canadian schooners in some of the international waters off Nova Scotia, particularly the Quero bank area. Naturally, the matter has been receiving close attention from this department and perhaps it may be well for me to give the house a brief factual outline of the position up to the present time.
The complaints which have been made to the department have come from the Canadian fishermen's union, of which Captain Ben McKenzie is the president, I understand, and Captain Willis Park the secretary-treasurer. The first message I received was from Captain Park, which reached me on May 21. In that telegram Captain Park protested, on behalf of the union headquarters at Lunenburg, against the action of foreign trawlers which, he said, were destroying Canadian gear by operating over grounds where fishermen from Lunenburg vessels had already set their trawl lines. Captain Park charged further that the trawlers disregarded signals and the buoys which marked the trawl lines. A day or so later I received from Mr. H. C. Meade, the union's district representative at Halifax, a message broadly similar to the one which Captain Park had sent.
Immediately on receipt of Captain Park's message we asked the department's chief supervisor at Halifax for a report. Subsequently, on June 1, Chief Supervisor Barry was also instructed to make contact with Captain Park and Mr. Meade and endeavour to obtain detailed statements from the masters of any of our schooners which had reported having gear destroyed or damaged. In this way we hoped to get definite information as to the identity of the trawlers which were alleged to have offended and as to the circumstances attending each incident. I may add, in passing, that at more or less the same time that these steps to gather information were being taken certain flights were made over the banks by planes of the Royal Canadian Air Force in order to observe the situation.
Fishing Operations

Pursuant to the instructions that he had been given to make contact with the union's representatives, Colonel Barry arranged to meet President McKenzie and Captain Park, and at Lunenburg on June 6 he gave them forms for statutory declarations to be made by the master and the mate of each schooner claiming to have suffered loss. He emphasized the importance of having the information in the declarations as complete and detailed as possible. Captain McKenzie and Captain Park said that a number of sworn declarations would be supplied to the department, but they pointed out that there might be some delay since declarations could be obtained only when the fishermen came in from sea between trips. Some delay was understandable, but I had hoped that it would not be quite so long. At all events, the first declarations given us by the union

ten in all-were not received by our Halifax office until Tuesday of last week, August 6, when they were at once sent on to Ottawa. The chief supervisor's office was given to understand by the union officers that several additional declarations would also be supplied, but so far they have not been received. Those already in the department have been made by the following individuals: Loran Riteey, master, and Michael Hackett, mate, schooner Dot tfc Hellie; Bernard Tanner, master, and Warren Selig, mate, schooner Fairmorse; Carmen Knock, master, and Ains-ley Hynick, mate, schooner Merilyn Clair; Willett Spindler, master, and John Barns, mate, Schooner Isabel Spindler; Magnus Slater, master and David Flett, mate, dragger Sea Nymph.
As yet we have not received any declaration from Captain Leo Corkum of the schooner Irene Mary who has been quoted in the press as charging deliberate destruction of his gear by a foreign trawler. One reason for the delay in making this statement has been my desire to have his declaration before me in view of the specific assertions attributed to him in the press.
My officials and I have studied the information contained in the declarations so far given the department by the fishermen's union. Por the moment I shall not discuss them except to point out that, while the declarations do set out certain destruction's as occurring at certain times, they fail completely to give us any definite information as to the identity or nationality of the trawlers alleged to have been involved in the particular incidents to which the statements relate.
In outline, then, these are the facts of the case up to the moment. I should add to them the statement that further detailed in-

vestigation of the whole matter is being carried on actively by the department and by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, both at sea and ashore.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie the house adjourned at 6.05 p.m.
Thursday, August 15, 1946
